# Connecting to your SensorStation {#connectivity}

Your SensorStation has a web server running locally on the Raspberry Pi, which means you can interact with your station by directly connecting via Ethernet or through a wireless connection. **Note that this is different than viewing your SensorStation via the CTT Web Portal**. The SensorStation Interface provides an overview of your station's operation, including real-time statistics on detections of tags and nodes, as well as controls to change settings, update your SensorStation software, toggle the cellular modem, and reboot the station. It is always best practice to connect directly to your SensorStation prior to deployment. From here you can run a station update, ensure your antennas are tuned to the expected task (detecting Nodes or Tags) and see in real-time that your station is detecting either as expected.

## Point-to-Point (P2P) Connection

A point-to-point connection lets you connect your computer directly to the SensorStation without needing a network, router, or internet access. This is the most reliable way to access your station in the field.

### Setting Up the Connection {-}

1. Plug one adapter into any USB port on your SensorStation.
2. Plug the other adapter into a USB port on your computer, and plug in the ethernet cable into the adapter.
  a. Alternatively, if your computer has an ethernet port, plug the ethernet cable directly into the ethernet port.
3. Wait up to **two minutes** for the SensorStation to acquire a link-local IP address.
4. Find the station's IP address using one of these methods:
    * Check the LCD screen: **Network > IP Address**
    * Try the hostname: `sensorstation.local`

The station will typically receive a link-local address in the `169.254.x.x` range. This address may change between connections. Once you have your IP address you can follow the [SSH instructions below.](#ssh-into-your-sensorstation)

### Troubleshooting the Connection {-}

If you cannot connect:

* Restart both your computer and the SensorStation, then try again.
* On some computers, you may need to disable WiFi temporarily so traffic routes over Ethernet.
* On the LCD, navigate to **Network > Ping** to verify whether the station sees any network connection.
* On Linux computers, go to Network Settings, and click the gear icon next to Wired. Select the IPv4 tab, and then select "Share to Other Computers". Click Apply.
* If using Windows, ensure the Ethernet adapter is recognized in **Network Connections**.

## Ethernet Connection

If you have an ethernet cable plugged into your network router, you can connect to the SensorStation as long as you are on the same network as the SensorStation.

### Before you get started you will need...

  * 2 USB to Ethernet adapters (we recommend: https://tinyurl.com/yc6llze4)
  * An Ethernet cable

### Making the Connection

  1. Connect each end of the Ethernet cable to the two USB->Ethernet adapters.
  2. Plug one USB end of an adapter into any of the USB ports on your SensorStation.
  3. Plug the USB end of the second adapter into your computer and wait up to two minutes to allow the SensorStation to acquire the IP address from your computer.
  4. You can test this connection through several diagnostics in the LCD menu.
    * `Network > Ping` will indicate a connection.
    * `Network > IP Address` will display a valid IP address.
  5. Open a web browser on your computer, and put the IP address from Step 5 into the URL window of the browser. The web interface should appear.
  6. Continue to [the SSH instructions below.](#ssh-into-your-sensorstation)


  *If for some reason you are unable to connect after Step 3, try restarting both the SensorStation and your computer and continue to Step 4.*

## WiFi Connection

**Note:**

::: {.version-v33 .version-v32 .version-v30}
  * The WiFi adapter is already built into your V3 board -- no extra adapter needed.
:::

::: {.version-v2}
  * V2 stations need a WiFi adapter like this one: https://store.celltracktech.com/products/wifi-usb-adapter-add-on-for-sensorstation-v2.
:::

You can also connect wirelessly to the station. Before you can do that, you need to connect the station to your WiFi network.

### Adding your WiFi Credentials to your SensorStation

#### Creating the JSON File

  1. In your code editor (i.e VSCode, TextEditor, etc.), create a new file and set the **Language Mode** to `JSON` and the **End of Line Sequence** to **LF** (for Line Feed).
  2. Type the following into the file:
  ```
    {
      "ssid":"my_ssid",
      "psk":"my_password"
    }
  ````

  **Make sure you change "my_ssid" to the name of your wifi network and "my_password" to the password for your wifi network! For example:**
  
  ```
    {
      "ssid": "MyHomeInternet",
      "psk": "ABC123"
    }
  ```

  3. Save the file and name it `credentials.json`.
  4. Create an empty folder on your USB thumb drive called `wifi`.
  5. Copy `credentials.json` file to the `wifi` folder.

##### WiFi Networks with No Password

If your WiFi network does not need a password, create a JSON file like above but only include the ssid:

```
  {
    "ssid":"my_ssid"
  }
```

1. Enable the WiFi module through the LCD screen by selecting Network > WiFi > Enable WiFi.
2. Plug the formatted USB drive into any of the SensorStation USB ports.
3. On the LCD screen, navigate to Network > WiFi > Mount USB. This will mount the USB drive onto the SensorStation. You should see a message saying "Mount: success"
  a. If you don't see that message, wait a few seconds and try again.
4. Hit the Back button, and then select "Get WiFi" from the same menu screen.
  a. If you are running an older disk image, you can Mount the USB drive through File Transfer > Mount USB, and then on the same screen select "Get WiFi".
  
## Transferring Files with SCP

SCP (Secure Copy Protocol) lets you transfer files between your computer and the SensorStation over the same connection used for SSH. This is useful for retrieving data files, downloading logs, or uploading configuration files without using a USB drive.

SCP is run on **your computer** through Terminal/Command Prompt, **NOT** on the SensorStation. Make sure you are not SSH'ed into the SensorStation; you should see something like `user@name-of-computer`, not `ctt@sensorstation`.

### SCP Basics

**Copy a file from the station to your computer:**

```bash
scp <username>@<station-address>:<remote-path> <local-path>
```

**Copy a file from your computer to the station:**

```bash
scp <local-path> <username>@<station-address>:<remote-path>
```

### Downloading Data Files {-}

Radio tag detection files are stored on the station under `/data/`. To download all current radio data files to a folder on your computer:

1. Open Terminal/Command Prompt

2. Create the folder `station-data` using:

```bash
mkdir station-data
```

3. Run the following commands:

::: {.version-v2}
```bash
scp -r pi@sensorstation.local:/data/ ./station-data/.
```
:::

::: {.version-v33 .version-v32 .version-v30}
```bash
scp -r ctt@sensorstation.local:/data/ ./station-data/.
```
:::

The `-r` flag copies directories recursively, so all files and subfolders are included.

### Using an IP Address Instead of Hostname {-}

If `sensorstation.local` does not resolve, use the IP address from the LCD screen:

```bash
scp -r ctt@169.254.12.34:/data/ ./station-data/
```

### SCP Tips {-}

* **Large transfers:** For stations with a lot of data, SCP over a point-to-point Ethernet connection is significantly faster than over WiFi.
* **Multiple stations:** If you manage multiple stations, the hostname `sensorstation.local` will resolve to whichever station is currently connected. You may see an SSH host key warning when switching between stations. To clear it, run:

```bash
ssh-keygen -R sensorstation.local
```

* **Windows users:** SCP is available natively in PowerShell and Command Prompt on Windows 10 and later. For older versions of Windows, install an SCP client such as [WinSCP](https://winscp.net) or [PuTTY's PSCP](https://www.putty.org).
* **Preserving timestamps:** Add the `-p` flag to preserve file modification times:

```bash
scp -rp ctt@sensorstation.local:/data/ ./station-data/
```

## SSH into your SensorStation

Besides accessing the station files, we can also access the station terminal through SSH.

SSH, or Secure Shell, gives you command-line access to the SensorStation's Raspberry Pi, allowing you to configure network settings, troubleshoot issues, run updates, and transfer files.

Open a Terminal (in Mac/Linux) or Command Prompt (in Windows) and run:

::: {.version-v33 .version-v32 .version-v30}
```bash
ssh ctt@sensorstation.local
```
:::

::: {.version-v2}
```bash
ssh pi@sensorstation.local
```
:::

Or using the IP address from the LCD screen:

::: {.version-v33 .version-v32 .version-v30}
```bash
ssh ctt@169.254.x.x
```
:::

::: {.version-v2}
```bash
ssh pi@169.254.x.x
```
:::

### First-Time Connection {-}

The first time you connect to a station, you will see a message like:

```
The authenticity of host 'sensorstation.local' can't be established.
ECDSA key fingerprint is SHA256:xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx.
Are you sure you want to continue connecting (yes/no)?
```

Type `yes` and press Enter. This saves the station's identity to your computer so you won't be asked again.

### Entering Your Password {-}

After accepting the host key, you will be prompted for a password. **The password will not appear on screen as you type** — this is normal. Type the password and press Enter. See the [SSH Credentials](#connecting-to-station) table above for your password.

## Common Commands to Run over SSH.

### Check if the Modem and WiFi are enabled

```bash
nmcli device status
```

### Update the SensorStation

This will pull the latest changes from the sensor-station-software repository on GitHub, and if you are on the 2.X.X image, it will update you to the latest disk image.

```bash
update-station
```

### Check if files are present

If you are unsure if the `SG_tag_database.sqlite` file was uploaded, you can check if the file is in the right folder using the following command:

```bash
ll /data/sg_files/
```
### Adding WiFi credentials

This is for SensorStations running disk images 1.4.0 and above. These disk images use NetworkManager to control the WiFi connection.

Look up available WiFi Networks
```bash
nmcli dev wifi list
```
Once you find your WiFi network name (aka the SSID) run:
```bash
sudo nmcli dev wifi connect "NetworkName" password "password"
```

Replace NetworkName with the WiFi network name (leave the quotes) and replace password with the password of the WiFi network (again, leave the quotes in the command). For example:

```bash
sudo nmcli dev wifi connect "MyHomeInternet" password "ABC123"
```

Then, run:
```bash
sudo nmcli c mod "MyHomeInternet" ipv4.method auto
```

This command edits the network connection profile so whenever the station boots up, it automatically tries to connect to your desired network.
